hints: Look at the circled flat part of the curve where pH rises only slowly, think about what mixture must be present halfway to neutralisation.
Recall which two organic containing particles exist when a weak acid like $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ is only partly neutralised by $\text{NaOH}$.
Think about what happens to added $\text{OH}^-$ ions in that mixture and how the acid dissociation equilibrium shifts to remove them.
walkthrough:
Picture what is in the flask in the flat region**
You are titrating ethanoic acid, $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}_2\text{H}$, with $\text{NaOH}$. At the start you have only the weak acid. At the equivalence point you have only the salt. In between, in the circled region, neutralisation is only partial. So you have leftover unreacted $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ together with the $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}_2^-$ ions just made by: $$\text{CH}_3\text{CO}_2\text{H} + \text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CO}_2^- + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$

Recognise the buffer mixture**
A weak acid plus its conjugate base together is exactly a buffer solution. That is why this part of the curve is flat. Buffers resist pH change when small amounts of acid or base are added.

Show how added alkali is removed**
When you add more $\text{NaOH}$, the $\text{OH}^-$ does not stay free to raise the pH sharply. It is consumed by the acid: $$\text{CH}_3\text{CO}_2\text{H} + \text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CO}_2^- + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$ You can also say it as $\text{OH}^-$ removes $\text{H}^+$, so the equilibrium $$\text{CH}_3\text{CO}_2\text{H} \rightleftharpoons \text{CH}_3\text{CO}_2^- + \text{H}^+$$ shifts to the right to replace $\text{H}^+$. Either way $[\text{H}^+]$ and therefore pH stays almost constant.

Final answer: Two species present: $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ and $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}_2^-$.
The mixture acts as a buffer solution so pH changes only slowly.
Added $\text{OH}^-$ / $\text{NaOH}$ reacts with $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ to form $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}_2^-$ and water, OR $\text{OH}^-$ removes $\text{H}^+$ and $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}_2\text{H} \rightleftharpoons \text{CH}_3\text{CO}_2^- + \text{H}^+$ shifts to the right.

hints: Think about what anion is left in solution once all the $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ has just been neutralised, and how that anion behaves with water.
walkthrough:
Explain the alkaline equivalence point**
Do not expect pH 7 here. This is a weak acid titrated with a strong base. At the equivalence point all $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ has become $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}_2^-$. That ion is the conjugate base of a weak acid, so it reacts slightly with water: $$\text{CH}_3\text{CO}_2^- + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightleftharpoons \text{CH}_3\text{CO}_2\text{H} + \text{OH}^-$$ The $\text{OH}^-$ made in this hydrolysis is why the measured equivalence point is around pH 9, well above 7.

Final answer: At the equivalence point only $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}_2^-$ (the conjugate base of a weak acid) is present with water, it hydrolyses to form $\text{OH}^-$: $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}_2^- + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightleftharpoons \text{CH}_3\text{CO}_2\text{H} + \text{OH}^-$, so pH > 7 as expected for a weak acid with a strong base.

hints: Start from the titre, calculate moles of $\text{MnO}_4^-$ used using $n = c \times V$ with volume in $\text{dm}^3$.
Combine the two half equations to find how many moles of $\text{V}^{2+}$ react with each mole of $\text{MnO}_4^-$, remember $\text{MnO}_4^-$ gains 5 electrons and $\text{V}^{2+}$ loses 3 electrons.
Link moles of $\text{V}^{2+}$ back 1:1 to $\text{VO}_2^+$ and to $\text{NH}_4\text{VO}_3$, then convert to mass using $M_r = 116.9$ and to percentage of the 0.150 g sample.
walkthrough:
Find moles of manganate(VII) used**
The titration oxidises all the $\text{V}^{2+}$ back to $\text{V}(+5)$. First get moles of the oxidant. The titre is $20.1 \text{ cm}^3 = 0.0201 \text{ dm}^3$ of $0.0250 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$ $\text{MnO}_4^-$: $$n(\text{MnO}_4^-) = c \times V = 0.0250 \times 0.0201 = 5.025 \times 10^{-4} \text{ mol}$$

Use electrons to get the reacting ratio**
Look at the half equations: $$\text{MnO}_4^- + 8\text{H}^+ + 5\text{e}^- \rightleftharpoons \text{Mn}^{2+} + 4\text{H}_2\text{O}$$ $$\text{V}^{2+} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{VO}_2^+ + 4\text{H}^+ + 3\text{e}^-$$ Each $\text{MnO}_4^-$ needs 5 electrons, each $\text{V}^{2+}$ supplies 3 electrons. So 3 $\text{MnO}_4^-$ react with 5 $\text{V}^{2+}$: $$n(\text{V}^{2+}) = n(\text{MnO}_4^-) \times \frac{5}{3} = 5.025 \times 10^{-4} \times \frac{5}{3} = 8.375 \times 10^{-4} \text{ mol}$$

Convert back to ammonium vanadate and find purity**
Zinc reduced every $\text{V}(+5)$ in $\text{VO}_2^+$ to one $\text{V}^{2+}$, so moles of $\text{NH}_4\text{VO}_3$ in the sample equals moles of $\text{V}^{2+}$ titrated: $$m(\text{NH}_4\text{VO}_3) = n \times M_r = 8.375 \times 10^{-4} \times 116.9 = 0.0979 \text{ g}$$ Then: $$\text{percentage purity} = \frac{0.0979}{0.150} \times 100 = 65.3\%$$ Keep 3 significant figures to match the data.

Final answer: moles $\text{MnO}_4^- = 0.0250 \times 0.0201 = 5.025 \times 10^{-4}$
moles $\text{V}^{2+} = 5.025 \times 10^{-4} \times 5/3 = 8.375 \times 10^{-4} = $ moles $\text{VO}_2^+ = $ moles $\text{NH}_4\text{VO}_3$
mass $\text{NH}_4\text{VO}_3 = 116.9 \times 8.375 \times 10^{-4} = 0.0979$ g
% purity $= 100 \times 0.0979 / 0.150 = 65.3$ % to 3 s.f.
